title: Bending and Impact Performance of Hybrid Sandwich Composites with Different Cellular Core Geometries
abstract: Abstract Sandwich composite structures with cellular cores offer significant potential for lightweight and high-performance engineering applications; however, the influence of core geometry on the combined stiffness–strength–energy absorption–weight balance remains insufficiently understood. In particular, systematic and mass-normalized comparisons of conventional, auxetic, and chiral core topologies manufactured under identical conditions are still limited in the literature. In this study, hybrid sandwich composites consisting of carbon fiber/epoxy skins and additively manufactured thermoplastic polyurethane cores with diverse cellular architectures—including honeycomb, grid, column, star-shaped, re-entrant, arc re-entrant, and hexachiral honeycomb geometries—were experimentally investigated. All cores were fabricated using fused deposition modeling with identical printing parameters to ensure fair comparison. The mechanical performance of the sandwich structures was evaluated through three-point bending and Charpy impact tests, focusing on bending strength, bending modulus, maximum displacement, impact energy, and impact strength. The results were analyzed using both absolute and mass-normalized metrics to assess true structural efficiency. The findings reveal that core geometry plays a dominant role in governing load-transfer mechanisms, deformation behavior, and energy absorption capacity. Among the investigated configurations, the hexachiral honeycomb core exhibited superior performance in terms of stiffness, strength, and impact energy absorption, while lightweight geometries such as honeycomb and grid cores demonstrated competitive specific performance after normalization. Auxetic geometries showed enhanced deformation capability but comparatively lower mass-normalized efficiency. The results provide clear experimental evidence that optimal sandwich core design requires simultaneous consideration of geometry and material efficiency, offering valuable guidelines for the development of lightweight, impact-resistant composite structures.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Composite materials are engineering materials formed by combining two or more distinct phases at the macroscopic scale, offering superior mechanical and physical properties compared to their individual constituents [ 1 ]. Owing to their high specific strength and stiffness, design flexibility, and corrosion resistance, composite materials have been widely used in advanced engineering applications, particularly in the aerospace, marine, automotive, and defense industries [ 2 ]. Among these materials, sandwich composite structures—consisting of two thin and stiff face sheets bonded to a thicker and lightweight core—have attracted significant attention due to their high specific bending stiffness (stiffness-to-weight ratio) and specific strength (strength-to-weight ratio) [ 3 ].

Sandwich composites can be classified based on the face-sheet materials as aluminum, steel, and laminated composite sandwich structures [ 4 ]. With respect to the core materials, they are commonly categorized as foam core sandwich structures [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 – 8 ] honeycomb sandwich structures [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ], corrugated sandwich structures [ 15 ,  16 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ], and lattice sandwich structures [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 ,  24 ,  25 – 26 ].

The mechanical behavior of the core material plays a critical role in determining the energy absorption capability of sandwich composites, particularly under impact loading. In this context, ductile core materials have attracted considerable attention due to their superior impact resistance. The high toughness associated with ductile materials, resulting from their ability to undergo large deformations, significantly enhances the impact resistance of sandwich composite structures [ 3 ]. Consequently, numerous studies have focused on investigating the impact behavior of sandwich composites. Usta et al. [ 27 ]examined the low-velocity impact behavior of sandwich composites with carbon fiber/epoxy (CFRP) face sheets and auxetic (negative Poisson’s ratio) and non-auxetic core geometries, where the core structures were fabricated from PLA using additive manufacturing. The influence of different core geometries on impact performance was systematically evaluated. Xie et al. [ 28 ] investigated sandwich structures with aluminum face sheets and foam honeycomb cores, demonstrating that an increase in core density led to a slight improvement in impact resistance. Xue et al. [ 29 ] studied the effect of core thickness on impact behavior and reported that core thickness had a negligible influence on the maximum impact force and absorbed energy. Wang et al. [ 30 ]analyzed the medium-velocity impact behavior of sandwich composites with aluminum face sheets and various core materials, including balsa wood and polypropylene honeycomb. Furthermore, Yang et al. [ 31 ] and Ugale et al. [ 32 ] examined the influence of carbon fiber and glass fiber face sheets on impact performance at different energy levels. Crupi et al. [ 33 ] investigated the effect of cell size on the impact behavior of sandwich composites with aluminum face sheets and aluminum honeycomb cores.

Thermoplastic polymers are increasingly used in sandwich composites due to their low density, high impact resistance, ease of processing and manufacturability, and recyclability [ 34 ]. Thermoplastics such as polypropylene (PP), polyamide (PA), polyetherimide (PEI), and polyetheretherketone (PEEK) are employed as face-sheet materials either in their neat form or reinforced with various fillers. Similarly, thermoplastic polymers including PP, PA, PEI, polymethacrylimide (PMI), PEEK, polyethylene terephthalate (PET), and polyethersulfone (PES) are widely used as core materials in sandwich composites. Among these, PP stands out due to its low production cost [ 34 ], widespread availability, and recyclability when used as both face-sheet and core material [ 35 ]. Although PMI is not melt-processable, its high thermal resistance up to approximately 180 °C has attracted significant research interest [ 36 ,  37 – 38 ]. Similarly, PEI has found extensive application as a thermoplastic sandwich core material owing to its operational temperature capability up to 180 °C and its excellent fire, smoke, and toxicity (FST) properties.

With recent advancements in additive manufacturing technologies, the fabrication of complex and functional core geometries for sandwich composites has become feasible. In particular, core structures produced by fused deposition modeling (FDM), such as lattice, honeycomb, corrugated, and auxetic geometries, have been extensively investigated for improving the mechanical, impact, and vibration performance of sandwich composites. The different core geometries employed in the present study and illustrated in Fig.  1  enable a systematic investigation of the influence of core architecture on the bending, impact, and dynamic responses of sandwich composite structures [ 27 ]. Fig. 1 Fabrication of the shell specimen using vacuum assisted resin infusion method

Among thermoplastic polymers, elastomeric materials have recently attracted growing attention for sandwich core applications, particularly in additively manufactured structures where large deformations and efficient energy absorption are required. Thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) has been increasingly employed as a compliant core material in additively manufactured sandwich composites due to its high ductility and energy absorption capability. Ahmed et al. investigated 3D-printed sandwich beams composed of TPU cores and rigid polymer face sheets, reporting that TPU-based cores significantly enhanced bending deformation capacity and delayed catastrophic failure under bending loads [ 39 ]. Jiang et al. [ 40 ] studied PLA/TPU sandwich structures produced by fused filament fabrication and demonstrated that the bending response was governed by the interfacial adhesion between TPU cores and brittle PLA skins, identifying interface debonding as the primary failure mechanism. Zhu et al. [ 41 ] examined orthogrid-based interlocking composite architectures incorporating compliant polymer cores and showed that mechanically interlocked interfaces improved load-transfer efficiency and stiffness compared to non-interlocked sandwich configurations. Gohar et al. [ 42 ] analyzed interlocked composite lattice structures under bending and confirmed that interlocking mechanisms promoted higher deformation tolerance and delayed failure, particularly when combined with ductile core materials. Ahmed et al. [ 39 ] further reported that sandwich beams fabricated with TPU cores and polyamide-based skins exhibited large mid-span deflections without interfacial failure, highlighting the role of TPU in accommodating shear deformation within the core region. These studies collectively demonstrate that TPU-based sandwich and composite systems provide superior deformation capability and energy absorption, while their overall mechanical efficiency remains strongly dependent on interface design and load-transfer mechanisms [ 39 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ].

Although sandwich composite structures with cellular and auxetic cores have been widely investigated, the current literature remains fragmented in terms of geometry-driven performance assessment and material efficiency. Most previous studies are restricted to a narrow set of core topologies and primarily report absolute mechanical properties, thereby overlooking mass-normalized metrics that are essential for lightweight structural optimization. Moreover, direct experimental comparisons of conventional, auxetic, and chiral core geometries manufactured under identical additive manufacturing conditions and integrated into hybrid composite sandwich systems are notably lacking. In particular, the coupled effects of core geometry, deformation mechanisms, and energy absorption on the stiffness–strength–weight balance have not been systematically quantified for elastomeric cores bonded to high-performance composite skins. To address these shortcomings, this study presents a comprehensive experimental investigation of sandwich composites comprising FDM-fabricated thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) cores with diverse cellular architectures and carbon fiber/epoxy skins. Flexural and Charpy impact responses are evaluated using both absolute and mass-normalized parameters, enabling a rigorous and geometry-independent assessment of structural efficiency.

sections.heading: Materials and Manufacturing
paragraphs: In this study, carbon fiber was employed as the reinforcing phase, while an epoxy-based resin was used as the matrix material for the fabrication of the shell structure. The composite plates utilized in the study were manufactured with a thickness of 1 mm using the vacuum infusion method (Fig.  1 ), consisting of an epoxy matrix reinforced with unidirectional (0°) carbon fibers. The resin system was prepared using a precision balance by mixing 66 wt% F1564 epoxy resin with 34 wt% F3486 hardener. The technical specifications of the F1564 epoxy resin and F3486 hardener are presented in Table  1 . Table 1 Technical data of the epoxy resin and hardener employed in the resin system F1564—epoxy F3486—hardener Viscosity (25 °C) 1200–1400 mPa-s 10–20 mPa-s Density (25 °C) 1.10–1.20 g/cm 3 0.94–0.95 g/c Mixing ratio %34 %66

The curing process was carried out at 60 °C for 8 h to ensure complete polymerization of the resin matrix and to achieve the final mechanical properties of the composite material. The fabricated composite plates were subsequently cut into shell specimens using a CNC machining system available at the laboratory facilities of Manisa Celal Bayar University. The specimens were machined to dimensions of 10 mm × 100 mm.

In this study, Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) was employed as the core material due to its widespread use in engineering applications, attributed to its high flexibility, impact resistance, abrasion resistance, and elastic recovery characteristics. The fabrication of the core structures followed the conventional stages of additive manufacturing processes. The core geometries investigated in this study (Fig.  2 ) consisted of full shape core, hexachiral honeycomb core [ 43 ], grid core, column core, arc re-entrant core, re-entrant core [ 44 ], honeycomb core [ 44 ], and star-shaped core configurations. Fig. 2 Geometrical configurations of the core structures

These geometries were selected based on key parameters known to influence the mechanical performance of sandwich composite structures, including infill ratio, geometric complexity, and load-transfer mechanisms. The primary objective was to comparatively evaluate the influence of different core geometries on the weight–strength balance and energy absorption behavior under identical material conditions.

Conventional cellular structures such as honeycomb, grid, and column cores were chosen as reference configurations due to their extensive investigation in the literature, ease of fabrication, and ability to provide uniform load distribution. Re-entrant and arc re-entrant cores, characterized by their negative Poisson’s ratio, were included for their enhanced flexibility and superior energy dissipation capability during deformation. These geometries were particularly selected to highlight the balance between lightweight design and deformation capability at low infill ratios (39–42%). Star-shaped and hexachiral honeycomb cores were incorporated owing to their complex architectures, multidirectional load paths, and aesthetically ordered geometrical arrangements. The infill ratios of these structures, ranging from 41 to 75%, were optimized to reflect their potential for high stiffness and enhanced energy absorption.

The fabrication of the core structures was carried out using a BASF-brand TPU filament (Ultrafuse ®  TPU 95A, BASF Forward AM, Germany) and an Ultimaker S5 3D printer. During the printing process, key parameters such as extrusion temperature, printing speed, build plate temperature, infill ratio, and layer thickness were carefully controlled to ensure adequate interlayer bonding. The 3D printing parameters employed in this study are presented in detail in Table  2 . To ensure process repeatability, identical printing parameters were applied to all core components produced for the composite structures. Table 2 Additive manufacturing parameters used for core fabrication Nozzle diameter 0.4 mm Wall loops 2 Printing temperature 230 °C Build plate temperature 65 °C Orientation angle 45°, −45° Layer thickness 0.12 mm Printing speed 90 mm/s

The shell and core materials were bonded using the same epoxy resin employed in the fabrication of the shell material, ensuring uniform load transfer across all specimens. A schematic technical drawing of the test specimen, including its dimensions, is presented in Fig.  3 . The specimens had a length of 100 mm and a width of 10 mm, with a shell thickness of 1 mm and a core thickness of 20 mm, resulting in a total thickness of 22 mm. The test specimens prepared for mechanical testing are shown in Fig.  4 . Fig. 3 Technical drawing of specimens Fig. 4 Test specimens

sections.heading: Bending Test
paragraphs: The three-point bending tests of the specimens were conducted using a Shimadzu AG-IS universal testing machine with a load capacity of 100 kN (Autograph), as shown in Fig.  5 . The testing system is a high-precision servo-hydraulic machine capable of operating under load-controlled, displacement-controlled, or strain-controlled modes. All tests were performed using a three-point bending fixture mounted on the testing machine. In accordance with the ASTM D790 standard, ten specimens were tested for each configuration. The span length between the lower supports ( L ) was set to 80 mm in accordance with the specimen dimensions and the ASTM D790 standard. Fig. 5 Schematic representation of the bending test

From the bending tests, the maximum bending strength ( σ _max), bending modulus ( E ), and maximum displacement ( δ _max) values were determined. The maximum bending strength represents the highest stress sustained by the material at failure and serves as an indicator of the load-carrying capacity of the structure. The bending modulus reflects the stiffness of the material, corresponding to its resistance to elastic deformation; higher modulus values indicate lower deformation under bending loads. The maximum displacement quantifies the deformation experienced by the structure under loading and is a critical parameter for assessing the energy absorption capability of the core structure.

The mechanical data obtained enabled a comprehensive evaluation of the load-bearing capacity, stiffness, and deformation behavior of the shell–core system. In particular, the experimental characterization of structures fabricated via the hybrid manufacturing approach is essential for assessing the applicability and performance potential of the proposed method in engineering applications. Consequently, the ASTM D790-compliant bending test served not only as a material characterization technique but also as a fundamental tool for evaluating the mechanical response of the developed hybrid structures under loading conditions representative of real-world applications.

sections.heading: Charpy Impact Test
paragraphs: To determine the impact resistance of the specimens, a MITECH XJU-22 digital Charpy/Izod impact testing machine was employed. This device is a pendulum-type semi-automatic impact testing system developed in accordance with the ASTM D6110 standard. In the present study, the Charpy configuration (simply supported beam type) was selected to measure the energy required to fracture the specimens. For each configuration, ten specimens were tested in accordance with the ASTM D6110 standard to ensure statistical reliability.

During the test, the pendulum arm was raised to a predetermined potential energy level and subsequently released. The released pendulum struck the specimen at its mid-span with a defined velocity, and the fracture energy ( E ) was automatically recorded in Joules (J) via the digital display of the testing machine. The measured energy value represents the impact resistance of the material. The experimental results were statistically evaluated using the sample standard deviation approach

These tests were conducted to determine the impact toughness of the materials and to comparatively evaluate the energy absorption behavior of composite sandwich structures with different core geometries. During testing, unnotched specimens were fractured under a single impact using a pendulum hammer of a defined mass. The energy absorbed by the specimen was calculated as the energy lost by the hammer during fracture and was expressed in Joules.

The absorbed energy provides direct insight into the material’s toughness and impact resistance under sudden loading conditions. Unnotched Charpy testing is particularly suitable for complex composite systems, such as shell–core hybrid structures, as it reveals how the entire structural assembly carries and dissipates impact loads prior to crack initiation. In the context of this study, the unnotched Charpy test enabled a quantitative assessment of the impact performance of different shell–core combinations under dynamic loading. The results highlight both the impact resistance and energy absorption capacity of the hybrid structures, while also demonstrating the contribution of shell–core interaction to overall structural integrity. The use of unnotched specimens allowed the natural fracture behavior of the materials to be observed, providing critical insight into the mechanical advantages of the proposed hybrid manufacturing approach.

sections.heading: Results and Discussions
paragraphs: In this study, the mechanical performances of the cellular core geometries were evaluated using the full shape core specimen as a reference in the graphical comparisons. The primary purpose of including the full shape core in the graphs was to enable a relative assessment of the strength, stiffness, and energy absorption capacities provided by the cellular architectures with respect to the solid (non-porous) configuration fabricated from the same material. This approach allows the influence of geometric design on mechanical behavior to be more clearly distinguished from material-dependent properties. Consequently, the effect of core topology on the overall mechanical response can be evaluated in a more systematic and unbiased manner, highlighting the role of structural design in enhancing performance beyond the intrinsic characteristics of the base material.

sections.heading: Bending Results
paragraphs: In this study, the bending behaviors of different core geometries produced via the hybrid manufacturing approach were evaluated through a combined assessment of experimental results and post-manufacturing physical observations. The deformation and failure modes observed during testing are illustrated in Fig.  9 . Since the core structures were fabricated from thermoplastic polyurethane using additive manufacturing, not only the load-bearing characteristics of the geometry but also manufacturing-related factors—such as printing traces, interlayer integrity, and continuity of the cell walls—had a direct influence on the bending performance. For each geometry, the expected mechanical response was interpreted in conjunction with the experimentally observed manufacturing effects, ensuring consistency with the graphical data.

Figure  6  presents the bending strength values obtained from the bending tests of the cellular core geometries. According to the experimental findings, pronounced performance differences were observed among the cellular structures, indicating that each geometry exhibits a distinct load-transfer mechanism that significantly affects bending strength. Fig. 6 Bending strength and mass-normalized bending strength results of the core geometries

The re-entrant (auxetic) structure exhibited a bending strength of 3.70 MPa. Although its negative Poisson’s ratio provided a certain degree of stability during deformation, surface irregularities and layer discontinuities formed at joint regions during fabrication limited its overall performance as visually confirmed in Fig.  9 . Variations in strut diameters and minor manufacturing defects observed at corner regions contributed to the moderate bending strength of the re-entrant geometry.

The column-type structure demonstrated the lowest bending strength in this series, with a value of 1.70 MPa. This result can be attributed to the inherent susceptibility of the elongated cell walls to buckling under bending loads. Additive manufacturing-induced issues, such as non-uniform layer deposition, surface roughness, and cross-sectional discontinuities, further accelerated premature damage. This behavior is also evident from the failure patterns shown in Fig.  9 . The inability of the column geometry to establish a stable load-transfer path under bending loading explains its inferior performance.

The arc re-entrant structure exhibited a bending strength of 3.62 MPa. Owing to its curved cell walls, this geometry was capable of distributing loads along the arc paths and displayed a deformation behavior similar to that of the re-entrant structure. However, cross-sectional irregularities observed at the cell junctions restricted effective load transfer, resulting in an overall moderate bending response.

The star-shaped cellular geometry produced a bending strength of 3.75 MPa, corresponding to a moderate-to-low performance level. Stress concentrations at the sharp tips of the star-shaped topology, combined with partially filled sections at certain junctions, reduced the load-carrying capacity. Additionally, the cell tips exhibited a tendency toward early crack initiation under bending loads. These crack initiation sites can be observed in Fig.  9 .

The honeycomb geometry achieved a bending strength of 3.64 MPa, representing a moderate performance among the tested structures. Although the hexagonal cells theoretically promote efficient load distribution, minor irregularities in the cell walls and layer orientation effects introduced during fabrication limited the achievable strength. Nevertheless, the honeycomb structure exhibited a stable and balanced deformation behavior during bending testing.

The grid geometry showed a bending strength of 3.60 MPa, yielding performance comparable to that of the honeycomb structure. Stress concentrations at the corner regions of the grid cells, exacerbated by slight manufacturing defects at these locations, contributed to strength reduction. During testing, the grid structure demonstrated a relatively rigid global deformation response; however, crack initiation at peak stress locations occurred at an accelerated rate.

In contrast, the hexachiral honeycomb structure achieved the highest bending strength among all tested geometries, reaching a value of 5.69 MPa. The stable cellular arrangement based on axial load transfer enabled effective force transmission along the struts during bending, thereby reducing deformation and delaying crack initiation. The continuity of the joints and the relatively uniform filling of the cell walls as clearly seen in Fig.  9 , as observed in the physical specimens, strongly support this superior performance.

Overall, the hexachiral honeycomb structure—characterized by a dominant axial load-bearing mechanism—emerged as the most structurally efficient geometry, exhibiting the highest bending strength in the experimental tests as presented in the literatüre [ 45 ]. Honeycomb, grid, star-shaped, and re-entrant-derived geometries demonstrated moderate performance levels, whereas the column structure exhibited significantly inferior behavior. These results clearly indicate that core geometry plays a decisive role in determining bending strength, while the quality of additive manufacturing equally exerts a critical influence on the final mechanical performance of the structures. The distinct deformation modes of each geometry are comparatively shown in Fig.  9 .

When the non-normalized bending strength values are evaluated together with the mass-normalized bending strength results, significant differences emerge in terms of understanding the true mechanical efficiency of the core geometries. Normalization provides a fairer basis for comparison by revealing not only the absolute strength of each structure but also its load-carrying capacity per unit mass.

In the non-normalized results, the hexachiral honeycomb (11.76 MPa) and honeycomb (10.97 MPa) geometries exhibited the highest bending strength values, followed by the grid (8.69 MPa), re-entrant (8.65 MPa), arc re-entrant (8.88 MPa), and star-shaped (9.21 MPa) structures. This ranking is primarily governed by the intrinsic load-transfer mechanisms of the geometries. In particular, the axial load-bearing behavior and well-distributed nodal connectivity in the hexachiral honeycomb and honeycomb topologies enable efficient force transmission, resulting in superior bending strength.

In contrast, the mass-normalized bending strength ranking exhibited noticeable changes, highlighting that relatively lightweight geometries can offer higher load-bearing efficiency on a per-mass basis. The hexachiral honeycomb structure maintained the highest performance in both absolute and normalized results, indicating that this topology is not only mechanically robust but also highly efficient in terms of material utilization. Although the honeycomb geometry achieved bending strength values close to those of the hexachiral honeycomb in absolute terms, a slight reduction was observed in the normalized results. This behavior can be attributed to localized stability limitations under bending, despite the lightweight nature of the thin cell walls.

More pronounced shifts were observed for the grid, star-shaped, and particularly the re-entrant and arc re-entrant geometries. While these structures demonstrated moderate bending strength in the non-normalized comparison, their efficiency became more evident in the mass-normalized analysis, with some configurations yielding more competitive results than initially expected. Specifically, the re-entrant and arc re-entrant structures benefited from their auxetic deformation characteristics, which enabled effective material utilization and resulted in higher-than-anticipated strength per unit mass.

Conversely, the column geometry exhibited poor performance in both non-normalized and normalized evaluations. This outcome is attributed to the susceptibility of the long, slender columns to buckling, which not only limits absolute strength but also leads to inefficient strength-to-weight performance.

The comparative assessment of these two graphs clearly demonstrates that core geometry optimization should address not only absolute strength but also the balance between lightweight design and mechanical efficiency. While the non-normalized results reflect the maximum load-bearing capacity, the mass-normalized analysis reveals the specific load-carrying performance that is critical for engineering applications. Overall, hexachiral honeycomb and honeycomb structures preserve their high-performance potential, whereas auxetic-based geometries prove to be more advantageous in terms of material efficiency than initially anticipated. This comparison underscores the importance of normalization as a critical step in the design of lightweight and mechanically efficient core structures.

Figure  7  presents the bending modulus results (elastic stiffness modulus in MPa) of each core geometry. Examination of the results reveals pronounced differences in stiffness among the geometries, with the hexachiral honeycomb structure clearly outperforming all other cellular configurations. Fig. 7 Bending modulus and mass-normalized bending modulus results of the core geometries

According to the experimental results, the bending modulus ranking is as follows: hexachiral honeycomb (34.11 MPa); grid (15 MPa); honeycomb (12.85 MPa); star-shaped (9.35 MPa); column (10.35 MPa); re-entrant (1.32 MPa); arc re-entrant (1.28 MPa).

The hexachiral honeycomb geometry exhibited the highest bending modulus by a significant margin, reaching 34.11 MPa. In this topology, the short cell walls transfer stresses directly through an axial load-carrying mechanism, resulting in high stiffness within the elastic region. The continuity of the joints and the inherent geometric stability limit deformation under bending loads, making this configuration the stiffest among the tested structures.

The grid geometry ranked second with a bending modulus of 15 MPa. Although load transfer at the joints is less efficient compared to the hexachiral honeycomb, the four-directional symmetric arrangement provides relatively stable elastic behavior. Minor manufacturing traces observed at the cell corners slightly limited the modulus; however, the overall structural arrangement supported stiffness.

The honeycomb geometry achieved a bending modulus of 12.85 MPa, placing it third. Due to the ability of hexagonal cells to distribute loads in-plane, honeycomb structures are theoretically expected to exhibit high specific stiffness. Nevertheless, surface undulations and slight variations in cell wall thickness inherent to FDM manufacturing reduced the stiffness relative to the hexachiral honeycomb geometry.

The star-shaped geometry demonstrated a moderate stiffness of 9.35 MPa. Stress concentration at sharp cell tips and discontinuities in load transfer are inherent to this topology, which explains the reduced elastic modulus. In addition, partially filled sections at joint regions negatively affected stiffness.

The column-based geometry exhibited a bending modulus of 10.35 MPa, comparable to that of the star-shaped structure. This configuration tends to behave more flexibly even within the elastic region, as the long columns possess low geometric stability. In FDM production, layer discontinuities and cross-sectional fluctuations in such thin-walled structures play a significant role in limiting the elastic modulus.

The re-entrant (1.32 MPa) and arc re-entrant (1.28 MPa) structures exhibited significantly lower bending modulus values. This behavior is attributed to the cell angles of auxetic structures, which allow lateral expansion within the elastic region. Since the negative Poisson’s ratio effect enhances deformability rather than stiffness, the low modulus values are consistent with the expected mechanical response. The curvature of the struts and the cell geometry permit greater elastic deformation, thereby reducing stiffness.

Manufacturing quality also directly influenced the measured modulus values. In FDM-based fabrication, parameters such as layer height, extrusion rate, continuity of cell walls, and surface roughness play a critical role in determining elastic stiffness. Thin-walled cellular structures are particularly sensitive to interlayer bonding quality, making their modulus values more susceptible to manufacturing-induced defects. Furthermore, microscopic stiffened regions and residual stresses at the core–skin interface also contributed to variations in the measured modulus.

Overall, the hexachiral honeycomb geometry formed the stiffest structure, while the honeycomb and grid geometries provided moderate stiffness [ 46 ]. In contrast, auxetic structures remained at low modulus levels due to their deformation-oriented mechanical characteristics [ 47 ]. These findings indicate that hexachiral honeycomb and honeycomb geometries are more suitable for applications requiring high stiffness, whereas auxetic structures may be preferred in applications where enhanced deformability is desired.

When the non-normalized bending modulus values are evaluated together with the mass-normalized bending modulus results shown in Fig.  7 , a significant change in the true efficiency ranking of the cellular core geometries in terms of elastic stiffness becomes evident. Although bending modulus is a critical parameter representing the elastic stiffness of a structure, absolute values alone can be misleading in terms of material efficiency, since different geometries require different amounts of material during fabrication. Therefore, normalization of modulus values with respect to mass is essential to reveal the stiffness provided per unit weight of the structure.

In the non-normalized results, the full shape (97.20 MPa) and hexachiral honeycomb (70.50 MPa) geometries exhibited the highest bending modulus values by a large margin, followed by the honeycomb (38.71 MPa), grid (36.23 MPa), column (27.36 MPa), and star-shaped (22.96 MPa) structures, while the re-entrant and arc re-entrant geometries showed very low values. Although this ranking reflects the intrinsic load-bearing mechanisms of the geometries, it neglects the amount of material required by each structure to achieve this stiffness.

The mass-normalized bending modulus graph in Fig.  7  reorganizes this ranking from a more engineering-oriented perspective. In the normalized results, the hexachiral honeycomb structure once again demonstrated the highest performance, proving to be the most efficient geometry not only in terms of absolute stiffness but also in stiffness-to-weight efficiency. In the hexachiral honeycomb topology, the short cell walls and strong nodal continuity enable higher stiffness to be achieved with less material, explaining its consistent superiority in both absolute and normalized evaluations.

The honeycomb and grid geometries maintained moderate-to-high performance in the normalized results. Both structures exhibit stable elastic behavior due to their regular cellular architectures; however, they do not reach the stiffness efficiency level of the hexachiral honeycomb. This is attributed to lower axiality of load transfer under bending and higher material usage compared to the hexachiral honeycomb configuration.

A particularly notable outcome is observed for the re-entrant and arc re-entrant geometries. Despite being relatively lightweight, these auxetic structures exhibit low stiffness efficiency even after normalization. This behavior indicates that the cell angles enabling elastic expansion inherently limit stiffness generation. Consequently, re-entrant and arc re-entrant geometries are unsuitable for stiffness-critical applications, even when weight reduction is a priority.

The star-shaped and column geometries occupy the lower-middle range in the normalized graph and demonstrate lower stiffness efficiency compared to the hexachiral honeycomb, grid, and honeycomb structures. In particular, the column structure fails to compensate for its low modulus despite its low weight, as the long cell struts are mechanically weak against elastic deformation, which is directly reflected in the normalized results.

In conclusion, the comparative evaluation of the bending modulus graph and its mass-normalized counterpart clearly demonstrates that the hexachiral honeycomb geometry not only provides high stiffness but does so with the highest material efficiency [ 48 ]. While honeycomb and grid structures offer balanced performance, auxetic geometries remain inefficient in terms of stiffness [ 10 ,  14 ]. This comparison highlights the critical importance of geometric optimization in stiffness-driven lightweight structural design and emphasizes that core selection should be based not only on absolute performance metrics but also on specific stiffness (stiffness-to-weight) criteria.

Figure  8  presents the maximum displacement values (in mm) obtained for each core geometry. The maximum displacement represents the largest deformation reached by the specimen under bending loading before failure. Lower displacement values indicate a stiffer structure with higher resistance to deformation, whereas higher values reflect a more compliant behavior with greater deformation capability. According to the experimental results, the maximum displacement values were recorded as follows: column 22.39 mm; honeycomb 21.00 mm; star-shaped 16.39 mm; grid 16.90 mm; re-entrant 11.95 mm; arc re-entrant 12.51 mm; and hexachiral honeycomb 9.07 mm. Fig. 8 Maximum displacement results of the core geometries

The column geometry exhibited the highest maximum displacement value of 22.39 mm. This result confirms that the topology composed of slender and elongated columns undergoes significant deformation under bending loads and displays low stiffness. The tendency of long columns to transition from the elastic to the plastic regime at lower load levels contributed to the high displacement values. In addition, weak interlayer bonding inherent to additively manufactured thin columns facilitated the progression of deformation.

The honeycomb geometry showed the second-highest displacement value at 21.00 mm. This behavior is attributed to the elastic flexibility provided by the hexagonal cell walls, which allow a certain degree of deformation under bending. The moderate stiffness of the honeycomb structure arises from partial rotation of the cell walls during loading; however, the deformation remained relatively stable and did not lead to abrupt failure.

The star-shaped geometry exhibited a moderately high displacement of 16.39 mm. The elongated and sharp cell arms of the star-shaped topology lead to stress concentration during bending, accelerating deformation in these regions. Cross-sectional irregularities observed at the junction points further reduced the resistance of the structure to deformation.

Similarly, the grid geometry demonstrated a displacement of 16.90 mm, comparable to that of the star-shaped structure. In grid cells, corner regions act as critical load-transfer zones, where displacement increases rapidly under bending loads. Consequently, the grid geometry exhibited moderate stiffness accompanied by a noticeable deformation capacity.

The re-entrant (11.95 mm) and arc re-entrant (12.51 mm) structures showed intermediate maximum displacement values. Owing to their auxetic nature, these geometries possess cell angles that tend to expand during bending, enabling deformation to be distributed over a wider region while remaining controlled within the elastic regime. As a result, the displacement values of auxetic structures were neither excessively high nor low, reflecting a balanced behavior between flexibility and deformation control.

The hexachiral honeycomb geometry exhibited the lowest maximum displacement value of 9.07 mm, indicating the highest stiffness among all tested structures. The short struts and high axial load-carrying capacity of the hexachiral honeycomb topology significantly restricted global deformation under bending loads. The direct transmission of loads along the cell walls limited deformation progression prior to failure.

Visual inspection of the specimens revealed that structures exhibiting high displacement values, particularly the column and honeycomb geometries, contained a higher density of micro-voids, surface roughness, and visible interlayer boundaries on the strut surfaces. These features acted as localized deformation initiation sites, accelerating deformation under bending. In contrast, the high continuity of cell walls observed in the hexachiral honeycomb and grid geometries suppressed the formation of localized deformation zones, resulting in lower displacement values.

Overall, the column and honeycomb structures displayed the most compliant behavior [ 49 ], whereas the hexachiral honeycomb geometry exhibited the stiffest response under bending. The re-entrant and arc re-entrant geometries provided moderate deformation capability, while the grid and star-shaped structures demonstrated intermediate behavior [ 50 ]. These findings clearly indicate that core geometry is a decisive parameter governing deformation mechanisms under bending loads (Fig.  9 ). Fig. 9 Images of the specimens before and after bending test

sections.heading: Charpy Impact Results
paragraphs: Figure  10  presents the Charpy impact energy (J) and mass-normalized Charpy impact energy (J/g) results of the specimens, respectively. These values represent the total energy absorbed by the specimens prior to fracture under impact loading and provide direct insight into the ductility, fracture resistance, and energy dissipation capability of the structures. According to the experimental measurements, the impact energy values were obtained as follows: hexachiral honeycomb 15.42 J; honeycomb 5.45 J; star-shaped 5.36 J; arc re-entrant 5.05 J; re-entrant 4.92 J; grid 5.99 J; and column 4.28 J. Fig. 10 Charpy impact energy and mass-normalized Charpy impact energy values obtained for different core geometries

The hexachiral honeycomb structure exhibited a significantly higher impact energy absorption capacity than all other geometries, reaching 15.42 J. The axial load-transfer mechanism inherent to the hexachiral honeycomb topology enables the impact load to be distributed simultaneously along multiple cell walls, allowing substantially greater energy storage prior to fracture. The continuity at the node regions and the stable behavior of the short struts further enhance the ductile impact response of the hexachiral honeycomb structure. These results demonstrate that the hexachiral honeycomb geometry is not only highly stiff but also possesses outstanding energy absorption capability under impact loading.

The honeycomb geometry showed one of the second-highest impact energy values at 5.45 J. The hexagonal cell arrangement distributes the impact load relatively uniformly across the cell walls, resulting in a controlled fracture mechanism. However, compared to the hexachiral honeycomb geometry, the honeycomb structure exhibits weaker strut continuity and greater susceptibility of the cell walls to bending, which promotes earlier damage initiation during impact.

The grid (5.99 J), star-shaped (5.36 J), and arc re-entrant (5.05 J) geometries exhibited intermediate impact energy absorption behavior. In the grid structure, stress concentrations at corner regions accelerated crack initiation, while in the star-shaped geometry, sharp cell tips led to stress localization and localized crack propagation, limiting the overall energy absorption capacity. Although the auxetic nature of the arc re-entrant structure provided a certain degree of deformation capability during impact, the deformation was not sufficiently stable to ensure uniform energy dissipation, resulting in moderate impact performance.

The re-entrant structure exhibited an impact energy of 4.92 J, comparable to that of the arc re-entrant geometry. The auxetic cell angles allowed lateral expansion during deformation, contributing to energy absorption; however, curvature and cross-sectional irregularities in the struts hindered homogeneous load distribution, causing energy to concentrate within localized regions.

The column geometry displayed the lowest impact energy value of 4.28 J. The tendency of long and slender columns to buckle readily under impact loading prevented ductile energy absorption and led to a more brittle failure mode. Moreover, surface roughness, cross-sectional irregularities, and interlayer weaknesses inherent to FDM fabrication of thin walls promoted crack initiation, further reducing the impact energy.

It is well established that surface defects, microcracks, and cross-sectional discontinuities play a critical role in impact performance. Visual inspection revealed that small voids and incomplete fusion regions observed particularly in the column and re-entrant structures accelerated fracture during impact. In contrast, the superior continuity of cell walls in the hexachiral honeycomb structure enabled substantially higher energy absorption.

Overall, the results clearly indicate that the hexachiral honeycomb geometry significantly outperforms all other cellular structures in terms of impact energy absorption [ 48 ]. While honeycomb, star-shaped, grid, and auxetic-based geometries exhibit moderate impact performance [ 51 ], the column structure demonstrates the lowest energy absorption capacity [ 52 ]. These findings highlight that core geometry is a critical parameter governing energy dissipation mechanisms under impact loading.

Figure  11  presents the impact strength values per unit area (kJ/m 2 ) of the specimens. This parameter reflects the resistance of different core geometries to fracture under impact loading and indicates the ability of the cellular structure to absorb and redistribute the impact energy. Based on the measured values, the ranking is as follows: hexachiral honeycomb (25.1 kJ/m 2 ); re-entrant (23.0 kJ/m 2 ); arc re-entrant (22.1 kJ/m 2 ); grid (21.3 kJ/m 2 ); honeycomb (20.8 kJ/m 2 ); star-shaped (20.2 kJ/m 2 ); and column (19.4 kJ/m 2 ). Fig. 11 Charpy impact strength and mass-normalized Charpy impact strength results

The hexachiral honeycomb geometry exhibited the highest impact strength, reaching 25.1 kJ/m 2 . In this topology, the short struts and axially dominated load-transfer mechanism rapidly distribute the impact load along the cell walls, preventing the localization of stresses. This efficient and uniform load distribution is the primary reason for the superior impact resistance of the hexachiral honeycomb structure.

The re-entrant (23.0 kJ/m 2 ) and arc re-entrant (22.1 kJ/m 2 ) geometries also demonstrated high impact strength values. Due to their auxetic nature and negative Poisson’s ratio, these structures allow cell expansion during deformation, which facilitates the redistribution of impact energy throughout the cellular network and enables greater energy absorption prior to fracture. The slightly lower performance of the arc re-entrant geometry compared to the re-entrant structure can be attributed to localized stress intensification along the curved cell walls.

The grid geometry exhibited a moderate impact strength of 21.3 kJ/m 2 . In grid structures, corner regions act as critical stress concentration zones during impact loading. Nevertheless, owing to the four-directional load distribution provided by the grid topology, this geometry outperformed the star-shaped and column structures.

The honeycomb geometry showed an impact strength of 20.8 kJ/m 2 , which is very close to that of the grid structure. Although hexagonal architectures theoretically offer efficient multidirectional load distribution under impact, relatively thin cell walls in certain regions accelerated crack initiation and limited the overall impact resistance. As a result, the honeycomb structure provided a balanced but lower impact performance compared to the hexachiral honeycomb and auxetic geometries.

The star-shaped structure exhibited a moderate-to-low impact strength of 20.2 kJ/m 2 . The sharp cell tips inherent to the star-shaped topology promote stress concentration and act as crack initiation sites, thereby reducing impact resistance. The non-uniform load distribution in such geometries accelerates the fracture process under impact loading.

The column geometry demonstrated the lowest impact strength, with a value of 19.4 kJ/m 2 . Long and slender columns are highly susceptible to buckling under impact loads, which hinders efficient energy absorption and promotes abrupt, brittle fracture behavior. This result is consistent with the poor performance of the column geometry observed in both bending and impact tests.

Impact strength results are influenced not only by geometric design but also by factors such as the adhesion quality at the skin–core interface [ 53 ], micro-voids formed during manufacturing [ 54 ], incomplete infill regions, and surface irregularities. These defects serve as crack initiation sites under stress, leading to a more pronounced reduction in impact resistance, particularly in the column and star-shaped structures [ 55 ]. Therefore, optimizing impact performance requires the combined consideration of appropriate geometric design and high-quality manufacturing processes, including surface preparation and bonding quality.

When the non-normalized impact strength values (energy per unit area) are evaluated together with the mass-normalized impact strength results, it becomes evident that the true energy absorption efficiency of cellular core geometries under impact loading varies significantly depending on material usage. Although absolute impact strength reflects the maximum resistance of a structure under impact, the substantial differences in material consumption among different geometries limit the validity of direct comparisons based solely on absolute values. Therefore, mass normalization of impact strength provides a more objective assessment of structural efficiency by revealing the amount of energy dissipated per unit weight.

In the non-normalized impact strength results, the hexachiral honeycomb structure exhibited the highest performance (25.1 kJ/m 2 ), followed by the re-entrant (23.0 kJ/m 2 ), arc re-entrant (22.1 kJ/m 2 ), grid (21.3 kJ/m 2 ), honeycomb (20.8 kJ/m 2 ), star-shaped (20.2 kJ/m 2 ), and column (19.4 kJ/m 2 ) geometries. In this ranking, the manner in which the impact load is distributed across the cell walls, the locations of stress concentration, and the deformation capacity of each structure prior to fracture play a decisive role. However, since these results do not account for differences in structural mass, they provide limited insight into the specific impact strength of the geometries.

The ranking changes noticeably in the mass-normalized impact strength graph, where the material efficiency of lighter geometries becomes more apparent. The hexachiral honeycomb structure maintains its high performance even after normalization, demonstrating that it is the most efficient topology not only in terms of absolute impact resistance but also in terms of energy dissipation per unit mass. The short and robust struts of the hexachiral honeycomb geometry provide consistent superiority in both absolute and specific impact strength.

A notable observation is the shift in the relative positions of the honeycomb and grid geometries after normalization. While these structures exhibit moderate absolute impact strength, their relatively low mass results in higher-than-expected specific impact strength values. In particular, the low density of the honeycomb geometry leads to enhanced impact resistance per unit weight, whereas the four-directional symmetry of the grid structure allows a more balanced distribution of impact loads, yielding a relative performance gain in normalized results.

Although the re-entrant and arc re-entrant geometries demonstrate impact strength values close to that of the hexachiral honeycomb structure in the non-normalized graph, they partially lose this advantage in the normalized results. This behavior can be attributed to the inverse-angle configuration of auxetic geometries, which results in increased material accumulation within the cell struts. Consequently, despite their high deformation capability, the energy dissipation efficiency per unit mass of auxetic structures remains lower than that of lighter geometries such as the hexachiral honeycomb and honeycomb structures.

The star-shaped and column geometries exhibit low performance in both non-normalized and normalized graphs. In the star-shaped structure, sharp cell tips act as stress concentrators, while in the column geometry, the high buckling susceptibility of slender columns limits efficient energy absorption. As a result, both geometries display restricted specific impact strength.

In conclusion, the comparison of absolute and mass-normalized impact strength results demonstrates that geometries with high absolute impact resistance do not necessarily provide the highest specific performance [ 56 ]. Material efficiency therefore emerges as a critical parameter in design decisions. While the hexachiral honeycomb structure consistently outperforms other geometries in both absolute and normalized performance, lightweight geometries such as honeycomb and grid become more competitive after normalization [ 51 ]. In contrast, auxetic geometries, despite their apparent advantages in absolute impact strength, exhibit a relative decline in mass-normalized performance [ 57 ]. These findings clearly highlight that optimal performance under impact loading requires consideration not only of strength but also of the weight-to-strength ratio.

sections.heading: Mass Results
paragraphs: Figure  12  presents the mass values of each core geometry. Evaluation of the experimental data reveals a pronounced variation in mass among the geometries, indicating that cellular topology has a direct influence on material consumption. The measured mass values are as follows: honeycomb 7.8 g; column 8.89 g; star-shaped 9.57 g; arc re-entrant 9.58 g; grid 9.73 g; re-entrant 10.05 g; and hexachiral honeycomb 11.37 g. Fig. 12 Measured mass values of the different core geometries

The honeycomb geometry exhibited the lowest mass value at 7.8 g. Owing to the efficient arrangement of hexagonal cell walls, this topology achieves a given level of stiffness using a smaller amount of material. The honeycomb structure offers a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, making it particularly advantageous for studies focused on specific performance. The low mass of the honeycomb geometry is consistent with the widely reported characteristic of high mechanical efficiency combined with reduced material consumption.

The column geometry showed the second lowest mass, measuring 8.89 g. This structure consists of elongated cell struts and contains a relatively low material density within its cross-section, resulting in a lightweight architecture. However, this reduced mass was accompanied by lower stiffness and higher displacement values in mechanical tests, indicating that although slender column-based geometries are lightweight, their load-bearing capacity is limited.

The star-shaped (9.57 g) and arc re-entrant (9.58 g) geometries exhibited very similar mass values. Despite their complex multi-strut topologies, the relatively thin cell walls kept the overall mass at a moderate level. In the star-shaped structure, the presence of thin sections at the cell tips reduced material consumption, while in the arc re-entrant geometry, curved cell walls promoted a more uniform distribution of material.

The grid geometry produced a moderate mass of 9.73 g. Although material accumulation occurs at the corner regions of the quadrilateral cells, the balanced wall lengths limited excessive mass increase. As a result, the grid geometry provided a relatively stable balance between weight and load-bearing capability.

The re-entrant geometry exhibited an upper-mid range mass value of 10.05 g. The inverted angles and outward-bending struts that give rise to auxetic behavior resulted in locally thicker sections, increasing the overall mass of the structure. During fabrication, the inward bending of the cells led to localized increases in wall thickness, contributing to higher material usage.

The hexachiral honeycomb geometry exhibited the highest mass among all core topologies, reaching 11.37 g. In hexachiral honeycomb structures, cell walls are short but relatively thick, and additional material accumulates at the node regions. Furthermore, since load transfer predominantly occurs through axial struts, these walls are formed more robustly during fabrication. Consequently, despite exhibiting superior stiffness and strength, the hexachiral honeycomb structure resulted in the highest mass.

When interpreting the mass results, manufacturing-induced variability should also be considered. In FDM-based additive manufacturing, parameters such as filament flow rate, extrusion multiplier, toolpath width, and layer infill directly affect the final mass. Visual inspection revealed localized material accumulation along cell walls in some specimens, indicating that slight over-extrusion contributed to minor mass differences. Additionally, thin adhesive layers formed at the skin–core interface during bonding had a limited but non-negligible effect on the final mass.

Overall, the honeycomb, column, and star-shaped structures produced the lightest cores [ 58 ,  59 ], whereas the hexachiral honeycomb geometry exhibited the highest mass [ 60 ]. Re-entrant-type geometries occupied an intermediate-to-high mass range. These findings demonstrate that cellular core design plays a critical role not only in mechanical performance but also in weight optimization.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study experimentally investigated the effect of cellular core geometry on the bending and impact performance of additively manufactured sandwich composite structures. Conventional (honeycomb, grid, column, star-shaped), auxetic (re-entrant and arc re-entrant), and chiral (hexachiral honeycomb) core topologies were systematically compared under identical manufacturing and testing conditions to isolate the role of geometric architecture on structural response. The results clearly demonstrate that cellular geometry is a dominant design parameter governing stiffness, strength, deformation behavior, and energy absorption capacity of sandwich composites.

Among all investigated configurations, the hexachiral honeycomb core exhibited the highest bending strength, bending modulus, and Charpy impact strength in both absolute and mass-normalized terms. This superior performance is attributed to its short and axially loaded cell walls, which enable efficient load transfer and suppress localized stress concentrations under both quasi-static and impact loading. Auxetic cores (re-entrant and arc re-entrant) also showed enhanced impact resistance compared to conventional cores, owing to their negative Poisson’s ratio behavior that promotes deformation-induced energy dissipation. However, when normalized by mass, their relative efficiency decreased, highlighting the importance of considering material usage alongside absolute mechanical performance.

Conventional honeycomb and grid geometries demonstrated competitive mass-normalized impact performance despite moderate absolute strength values, emphasizing their structural efficiency in lightweight applications. In contrast, column and star-shaped cores consistently exhibited lower bending and impact performance, primarily due to buckling-prone slender members and stress concentration at sharp geometric features. These findings indicate that high absolute strength does not necessarily translate into optimal structural efficiency and that mass-normalized metrics are essential for objective performance comparison.

Overall, the results underline that the optimal design of sandwich composite cores subjected to bending and impact loads requires a careful balance between geometric complexity, load-transfer mechanisms, and material efficiency. The experimental framework and comparative insights presented in this study provide valuable guidance for the design of lightweight, impact-resistant sandwich structures in aerospace, automotive, and protective engineering applications.
